key_insight: The paper shows that pretraining data can be successfully poisoned even in realistic, large-scale, heterogeneous data pipelines—not just in controlled sources like Wikipedia. It highlights that data curation steps do not fully protect against these attacks.
problem_solved: It addresses the security gap in large language model pretraining, where malicious actors can insert harmful behaviors into training data in ways that are hard to detect, especially when data is filtered and curated at scale.
method: Demonstrates poisoning attacks beyond narrow, well-studied data sources by targeting more realistic pretraining corpora.
Examines how poisoned examples interact with data curation and filtering pipelines.
Shows that malicious behaviors can persist despite common dataset cleaning and selection procedures.
impact: This matters because it reveals a practical supply-chain risk for LMs: training data can be attacked before model training even begins. Practitioners may need stronger provenance tracking, anomaly detection, and defensive curation strategies.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram showing data source → curation/filtering → pretraining → model behavior, with poisoning injected at the source.
Side-by-side comparison of clean vs. poisoned training data and resulting model outputs.
Threat model icon set illustrating attacker, dataset, curation filter, and model.
Flowchart highlighting where standard defenses fail in large-scale preprocessing pipelines.
paper_title: Pretraining Data Can Be Poisoned through Computational Propaganda
paper_authors: Victoria Graf, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Noah A. Smith, David Kohlbrenner, Kyle Lo
